title: HTTP endpoints
text: HTTP endpoints These are internal application routes, not a public API. Every route below exists to serve Disband's own clients. They are authenticated by session cookie, are not versioned, and may change without notice. There is no API token scheme — see Building a bot .

title: HTTP endpoints
text: Route Method Purpose /api/stripe/create-checkout POST Creates an embedded Checkout session for basic or super . Promotion codes enabled. /api/stripe/portal GET Returns a Stripe billing portal URL. /api/stripe/sync POST Reconciles the caller's subscription directly from Stripe. /api/stripe/webhook POST Stripe events. Verifies the signature against STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET . /api/stripe/sync exists because a webhook is a single point of failure. If its URL or signing secret is wrong, a customer is charged and the app never learns about it. Reconciling on demand means a purchase applies even when the webhook never fires.

title: HTTP endpoints
text: Route Method Purpose /api/auth/signup-check POST Signup abuse checks. /api/profile/check-username GET Username availability. /api/moderation/access GET Whether the caller may use moderation tools. /api/moderation/platform-ban POST Platform-wide ban. Staff only. /api/moderation/restrict POST Applies an account restriction. Staff only.

title: HTTP endpoints
text: Route Method Purpose /api/link/preview GET Server-side link unfurling, so clients never fetch arbitrary URLs directly. /api/status GET Live service health. /api/releases GET Desktop release metadata. /api/bug-report POST Submits a bug report. /api/mobile-waitlist POST Mobile waitlist signup.

title: HTTP endpoints
text: There is deliberately no REST layer over the tables. Clients query Postgres through the Supabase SDK, and RLS decides what comes back: const { data, error } = await supabase .from("messages") .select("*, author:profiles(*)") .eq("channel_id", channelId) .order("created_at", { ascending: false }) .limit(50);

title: Architecture
text: Architecture Three clients, one backend, and very little bespoke server code.

title: Architecture
text: Web (Next.js) Desktop (Tauri) iOS (SwiftUI) | | | +--------- Supabase client SDKs --------+ | Postgres + Auth + Realtime + Storage | Next.js route handlers (Stripe, moderation, link previews, status) using the service role Most reads and writes go straight from the client to Postgres through the Supabase SDK, with Row Level Security deciding what is allowed. Server-side route handlers exist only where something must not be trusted to the client — verifying a Stripe webhook signature, or acting with elevated privileges. Because clients talk to the database directly, Row Level Security is the security model . Any rule enforced only in React or Swift is a convenience, not a control. See Security & RLS .

title: Architecture
text: Path Contains src/app/ App Router pages and API route handlers. src/components/discord/ The main chat surface — channel list, chat canvas, composer, modals. src/contexts/AppContext.tsx Central store: session, servers, channels, messages, friends, notes, realtime subscriptions. src/hooks/ Calls ( useCallManager ), subscriptions, media devices. src/lib/ Supabase clients, WebRTC helpers, theming, subscription entitlements. supabase/migrations/ Schema, RLS policies and RPCs, applied in filename order.

title: Architecture
text: Tauri wraps a static export of the web app. Two consequences worth knowing: The origin is tauri://localhost , so anything deriving a URL from window.location needs a fallback to the configured web app URL. Every external host the app talks to must be present in the CSP connect-src .

title: Architecture
text: A native SwiftUI app using supabase-swift and the same tables. It is not a web view. Themes are stored on the shared profiles.theme column, so a theme chosen on the phone applies on the web too.

title: Architecture
text: Calls are peer-to-peer WebRTC. Supabase Realtime carries only signalling — ring , accept , reject , cancel , offer , answer , ice , leave — and media never passes through the server. See Realtime for the channel layout.

title: Building a bot
text: Building a bot Planned Disband bots are self-hosted. You run the bot yourself, and a server owner invites it — the same way they invite a person. This is not built yet. As of v1.0.26 there are no bot accounts, no bot tokens, no invite flow and no gateway. Nothing in the codebase implements them. This page is the intended design, written down so it can be reviewed and built — not an API you can call today.

title: Building a bot
text: Step What happens 1. Create A developer registers a bot in Disband and receives a bot token. The token identifies the bot; it is not tied to a human account. 2. Self-host The developer runs the bot on their own machine or server. Disband does not host or execute bot code. 3. Invite A server owner opens the bot's invite link, sees the permissions it is asking for, and approves. The bot joins as a member. 4. Operate The bot connects to Disband with its token and acts only inside servers it was invited to, limited by the roles it was given. Why self-hosted Running bot code on Disband's infrastructure would mean executing untrusted programs next to user data. Self-hosting keeps that boundary clean: a bot is just a client holding a token, subject to the same permission checks as anyone else.

title: Building a bot
text: Bot developers never receive database credentials. A bot authenticates with its own token against Disband's API. It does not get Supabase project details, and it does not talk to Postgres directly. That boundary is the whole point — it means a bot's reach is defined by the permissions a server owner granted, and can be revoked by removing the bot. Worth being precise about one thing: the anon key shipped in Disband's own web and mobile clients is public by design — it is embedded in every build and grants nothing on its own, because Row Level Security decides what any request can actually read or write. It is not a secret, but it is also not a bot credential, and building an integration on it is not the supported path. See Security & RLS . The service role key is a different matter entirely. It bypasses RLS and grants full read and write access to every account and message on the instance. It must never be given to a bot, committed, or shipped to any client.

title: Building a bot
text: Everything below is illustrative. These endpoints do not exist. Authenticating Authorization: Bot <your-bot-token> Receiving events // Illustrative only. import { Client } from "@disband/bot"; // not published const client = new Client({ token: process.env.DISBAND_BOT_TOKEN }); client.on("messageCreate", async (message) => { if (message.author.bot) return; if (message.content !== "!ping") return; await message.reply("pong"); }); await client.connect(); Sending a message POST /api/v1/channels/:channelId/messages Authorization: Bot <token> Content-Type: application/json { "content": "Deploy finished", "reply_to_id": null } Permissions A bot's invite link declares the scopes it wants. The effective permission is the intersection of its requested scopes and the roles it holds in that server — a bot can never exceed what its roles allow. Scope Allows messages.read Receive messages in channels it can see. messages.write Post and reply. members.read Read the member list. channels.manage Create and edit channels.

title: Building a bot
section: What still has to be designed
text: Token issuance, rotation and revocation, and what a leaked token exposes. Whether events arrive over a persistent gateway or webhooks. How bots appear in the UI — a BOT tag, and a members-list grouping. Slash command registration and dispatch. Rate limits, per token and per server. Audit and removal: a server owner must be able to see what a bot did and revoke it in one action. Want to help build it? The honest starting point is schema and RLS — a bot identity that sidesteps the permission model would be worse than having no bot API at all. See Contributing .

title: Contributing
text: Contributing Conventions that matter in this codebase, mostly learned the hard way.

title: Contributing
text: Work on a branch and open a pull request into main . Run pnpm build and the TypeScript check before pushing. Match the surrounding code — naming, comment density and structure vary by area; follow the file you are in.

title: Contributing
text: Add a new numbered file in supabase/migrations/ . Never edit an applied migration. Make migrations idempotent: if not exists , create or replace , drop policy if exists . Enable RLS on every new table and write policies in the same migration. A table without policies is either invisible or wide open. To tighten an existing rule, rewrite the policy. Adding another permissive policy widens access, because Postgres OR s them.

title: Contributing
text: Enforce authorization in RLS or a security definer function. Treat client-side checks as cosmetic. Guard the inputs of security definer functions — RLS no longer protects them. Keep SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY server-side, always.

title: Contributing
text: Run xcodegen generate after adding or removing files; the .xcodeproj is generated and not committed. Retain RealtimeSubscription tokens returned by onBroadcast and onPostgresChange . Dropping one silently unregisters the callback. Prefer .task(id:) over withObservationTracking for lifecycle work. The latter fires once and re-registers asynchronously, so changes in the gap are lost.

title: Contributing
text: Set ack: true and check for "ok" before unsubscribing after a broadcast. Design signalling so crossed messages are survivable — treat cancel and leave as equivalent rather than binding each to one state.

title: Contributing
text: Prefer evidence over inference. When a change is visible, run the app and look at it; when it is a data change, query the database. Several bugs in this codebase looked like network problems and turned out to be a discarded callback token or a state flag reused for two meanings — reading the code alone would not have settled it.

title: Contributing
text: These pages are static HTML in disband-docs/ , with no build step. Edit a file, open it in a browser. If you document something that is not built, label it Planned and say so plainly — docs that describe imaginary features cost developers more time than missing docs.

title: Data model
text: Data model Every table lives in the public schema with Row Level Security enabled.

title: Data model
text: Table Purpose profiles One row per user, keyed to auth.users . Display name, username, avatar, banner, accent colours, status, theme, badge flags. friendships Requester/addressee pair with status pending , accepted or blocked . profile_change_log Backs per-plan rate limits on username and avatar changes.

title: Data model
text: Table Purpose servers Name, icon, banner, description, owner, invite code, discoverable flag. server_members Membership, with legacy role plus a role_id . server_roles Named roles carrying a JSON permission set. member_roles Many-to-many assignment of roles to members. channel_categories Ordered groupings for channels. channels text or voice , ordered by position . read_only marks announcement channels. server_bans Per-server bans.

title: Data model
text: Table Purpose messages Channel messages: content, attachment, reply target, edit timestamp. dm_threads / dm_messages 1:1 conversations. Threads are created only through an RPC. group_chats / group_chat_members / group_messages Multi-person chats outside any server. message_reactions Emoji reactions, keyed by context type so one table serves channels, DMs, groups and notes. notes Private notes. Every policy is auth.uid() = user_id ; there is no sharing path.

title: Data model
text: Table Purpose voice_presence Who is in which voice channel, with mute and deafen state. group_call_presence Equivalent for group calls. notifications / device_tokens In-app notifications and push registration. platform_bans / signup_ip_blocks / audit_log Platform moderation and an audit trail. bug_reports / mobile_waitlist / media_posts Supporting product surfaces.

title: Data model
text: Primary keys are uuid with gen_random_uuid() . Timestamps are timestamptz , defaulting to now() . Deletes cascade from the owning row — deleting a server removes its channels and messages. Columns are snake_case ; TypeScript and Swift models map them explicitly.

title: Running locally
text: Running locally Getting the web client running against a Supabase project.

title: Running locally
text: Tool Notes Node.js 20+ Next.js 16 requires a modern runtime. pnpm The repo ships a pnpm-lock.yaml ; other package managers will drift. Supabase project Postgres, Auth, Realtime and Storage. Xcode 16+ iOS client only.

title: Running locally
text: git clone https://github.com/polardev-ui/disband-latest.git cd disband-latest pnpm install

title: Running locally
text: Create .env.local . The app reads these at boot, so restart the dev server after editing. # Supabase NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL=https://<project>.supabase.co NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY=<anon key> SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY=<service role key> # server-side only # Stripe (billing) STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=sk_... NEXT_PUBLIC_STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=pk_... STRIPE_BASIC_PRICE_ID=price_... STRIPE_SUPER_PRICE_ID=price_... STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET=whsec_... NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL=http://localhost:3000 Never expose the service role key to the browser. It bypasses Row Level Security entirely. It must only appear in server-side code, and must never be prefixed NEXT_PUBLIC_ . A common setup mistake is putting a sk_live_… secret key in STRIPE_BASIC_PRICE_ID . Price IDs always start with price_ ; checkout fails with an opaque error otherwise.

title: Running locally
text: Migrations live in supabase/migrations/ and are applied in filename order. They are written to be idempotent ( if not exists , create or replace ), but check what a migration does before running it against data you care about. supabase db push

title: Running locally
text: pnpm dev # http://localhost:3000 pnpm build # production build pnpm lint

title: Running locally
text: The Xcode project is generated from project.yml by XcodeGen and is not checked in. Regenerate it whenever files are added or removed, or Xcode will not see them: cd ios xcodegen generate open DisbandiOS.xcodeproj Forgetting xcodegen generate after adding a Swift file produces confusing cannot find <Type> in scope errors for code that plainly exists on disk.

title: Introduction
text: Disband An open chat platform: servers, channels, direct messages, group chats, voice and video calls, and private notes — on web, desktop and iOS. This site documents how Disband is built and how to work on it. It is written for two audiences: people running or contributing to the codebase, and developers who want to build on top of it. Honest scope. These docs describe what Disband actually does today, at version 1.0.26. Where something is planned but not built — most importantly the bot API — it is labelled Planned and you will not find example code implying otherwise. Running locally Clone, configure Supabase and Stripe, and get a dev server up. Architecture How the Next.js app, Supabase backend and native clients fit together. Security model Row Level Security is the real authorization boundary, not the UI. Building a bot The proposed design — and why you cannot build one yet.

title: Introduction
text: Area Details Servers Channels grouped into categories, roles with granular permissions, invites, bans, discovery. Messaging Channel messages, DMs, group chats, replies, reactions, editing, attachments, polls, link previews. Voice & video 1:1 and group calls over WebRTC, with mute, deafen, camera and screen share. Notes A private, owner-only space for text and media. No sharing path exists. Subscriptions Free, Basic and Super tiers via Stripe, gating upload size, video quality and themes.

title: Introduction
text: Client Built with Web Next.js 16 (App Router, Turbopack), React 19, Tailwind CSS 4 Desktop Tauri, wrapping the exported web build iOS Native Swift and SwiftUI, with WebRTC for calls All three talk to the same Supabase project, so a change made on one appears on the others through realtime.

title: Realtime
text: Realtime Two mechanisms: Postgres change streams for data, and ephemeral broadcasts for signalling.

title: Realtime
text: Tables published to Realtime stream inserts, updates and deletes to subscribed clients. RLS applies, so a client only receives rows it is allowed to read. const channel = supabase .channel(`messages:${channelId}`) .on("postgres_changes", { event: "INSERT", schema: "public", table: "messages", filter: `channel_id=eq.${channelId}`, }, ({ new: message }) => append(message)) .subscribe();

title: Realtime
text: Topic Carries call-user:<userId> Inbound call signalling for one user: ring , accept , reject , cancel , leave . call:<callId> Negotiation between two peers already in a call: offer , answer , ice . typing:<scope> Typing indicators. The call id is derived deterministically from both user ids sorted and joined, so each side computes the same value without a round trip.

title: Realtime
text: Acknowledge broadcasts before unsubscribing. A send resolves as soon as the frame reaches the socket. If you unsubscribe immediately afterwards, the channel can be torn down before the server accepts the message, and it is silently dropped. Enable ack and wait for "ok" . const channel = supabase.channel(topic, { config: { broadcast: { self: false, ack: true } }, }); await subscribeChannel(channel); const status = await channel.send({ type: "broadcast", event, payload }); if (status !== "ok") throw new Error("broadcast not acknowledged"); await channel.unsubscribe(); On iOS, retain the subscription token. onBroadcast returns a RealtimeSubscription that cancels the callback when it deallocates. Discarding it leaves the channel subscribed but with no listener — everything looks healthy and no message ever arrives. // Store this; do not discard it. self.listenSubscription = channel.onBroadcast(event: "call") { json in handle(json) } try await channel.subscribeWithError()

title: Security & RLS
text: Security & RLS Clients hold a real Postgres session. Row Level Security, not the interface, decides what they can do. The UI is not a security control. Hiding a button stops an ordinary user from stumbling into an action. It stops nobody from calling the API directly. Every rule that matters must exist as an RLS policy or inside a security definer function.

title: Security & RLS
text: Server permissions resolve through member_has_server_permission(server_id, user_id, permission) . It: Refuses to answer for anyone but the caller, so it cannot be used to probe other users' permissions. Returns true immediately if the user owns the server — owners implicitly hold every permission. Otherwise resolves the member's roles and checks the permission flag. Permission Grants manage_channels Create, rename, reorder and delete channels and categories; post in announcement channels. manage_roles Create and assign roles. manage_server Edit server settings. manage_messages Delete other people's messages. kick / ban Remove or ban members. manage_emojis Manage custom emoji. mention_everyone Use @everyone and @here .

title: Security & RLS
text: Marking a channel read_only hides the composer. That alone would be trivial to bypass, so the rule lives in the insert policy: create policy "messages_insert" on public.messages for insert to authenticated with check ( auth.uid() = author_id and exists ( select 1 from public.channels c where c.id = messages.channel_id and public.is_server_member(c.server_id) and ( c.read_only = false or public.member_has_server_permission( c.server_id, auth.uid(), 'manage_channels') ) ) ); Postgres combines multiple permissive policies with OR . Adding a second policy to "tighten" a rule does the opposite — it widens access. To restrict, rewrite the existing policy or add a restrictive one.

title: Security & RLS
text: Operations that need to read beyond the caller's own rows run as security definer with a pinned search_path . They must guard their own inputs, because RLS no longer protects them. Examples include get_or_create_dm_thread , join_server_by_invite and list_discoverable_servers . Some columns are protected by triggers rather than policies: the badge flags on profiles are reset to their previous values on update, so a user cannot grant themselves a staff badge by writing to their own row.

title: Security & RLS
text: Key Where it may be used Anon key Client-side. Safe to ship — it grants nothing on its own, since RLS still applies. Service role key Server-side only. Bypasses RLS completely. Never send it to a browser.
